translationRepairs.before: During palace games Wu Di pointed out the boy to the witless Hui: 'That one is your heir.'
translationRepairs.after: Once he was playing on the palace steps with the imperial princes; when Emperor Hui came to audience, he took each prince's hand in turn; when he reached the crown prince, the emperor said, 'This is your son.'
translationRepairs.reason: Before invents "witless" and mistranslates 兒 as "heir," but the proposal wrongly makes Emperor Wu take the princes' hands; after 惠帝來朝 the hand-taking continues Hui's greeting, and 惠帝乃止 confirms he stopped that greeting when Wu said 是汝兒也.

translationRepairs.before: Pan Yue forged spirit-prayer lines; drunk Yu copied them under Chen Wu's orders.
translationRepairs.after: She had Gentleman of the Yellow Gate Pan Yue draft a prayer text mimicking the Crown Prince's usual intent; because he was drunk she made him copy it, having the young maid Chengfu bring paper, brush, and draft.
translationRepairs.reason: Before wrongly credits Chen Wu with ordering the copy; Chinese has Pan Yue draft the prayer-like text and 小婢承福 deliver paper, brush, and draft so the drunken Crown Prince writes it. The revision preserves his established title and renders 小婢 naturally.

translationRepairs.before: An imperial train stripped Yu at Eastern Palace.
translationRepairs.after: Thereupon Minister Director He Yu was dispatched with insignia, with Xie Jie as deputy, together with General-in-Chief Sima Tong, Prince of Liang; Eastern Garrison General Sima Yun, Prince of Huainan; Forward General Sima Dan, Eastern Martial Duke; Sima Lun, Prince of Zhao; and Grand Tutor He Shao. They went to the Eastern Palace to depose the Crown Prince as a commoner.
translationRepairs.reason: Before collapses the deposition embassy into a nameless "imperial train"; Chinese names 尚書和郁, 解結, 梁王肜, 淮南王允, 東武公澹, 趙王倫, and 太保何劭. The revision restores every envoy using their established full names and titles and makes the long list legible in English.

translationRepairs.before: Verses mocked Empress Nanfeng and Yu's childhood name.'
translationRepairs.after: Another went: 'South wind rises blowing white sand; far off Lu kingdom gloomy and tall; thousand-year skulls sprout teeth.'
translationRepairs.reason: Before replaces the rhyme with truncated commentary and a stray quote mark; Chinese quotes the full children's verse 南風起兮吹白沙…, which the proposed rendering restores.

translationRepairs.before: 'White Sand' was Yu's boyhood sobriquet.
translationRepairs.after: 'Shamen' was the crown prince's childhood byname.
translationRepairs.reason: 沙門 is the childhood byname Shamen; "White Sand" confuses it with 白沙 in the preceding rhyme, and the proposed "Shamen" restores the gloss.

translationRepairs.before: 'White Sand' was the crown prince's childhood byname.
translationRepairs.after: 'Shamen' was the crown prince's childhood byname.
translationRepairs.reason: The literal likewise misrenders 沙門 as "White Sand"; replacing it with "Shamen" matches the childhood byname in the Chinese gloss.

translationRepairs.before: After Lady Xie's mother died no one comforted him.
translationRepairs.after: Since the Lady of Yicheng died I received no comforting word—I constantly sat alone in empty rooms.
translationRepairs.reason: This sentence is still Yu's first-person letter; before shifts to third person and paraphrases away the title 宜城君, while the proposed wording keeps 自宜城君亡 and 不見存恤 in first person.

translationRepairs.before: When Deposed Commoner Jia died, they executed Liu Zhen, Sun Lü, Cheng Ju, and others, and posthumously restored the crown prince; the edict read: "The emperor dispatches the credential-bearer, concurrent Director of Works, Commandant of the Guard Yi Ce to the spirit of the late crown prince: Alas!
translationRepairs.after: When Deposed Commoner Jia died, they executed Liu Zhen, Sun Lü, Cheng Ju, and others, and posthumously restored the crown prince; the edict read: "The emperor dispatches the credential-bearer, concurrent Director of Works, Commandant of the Guard Yi to announce by patent to the spirit of the late crown prince: Alas!
translationRepairs.reason: In the patent formula 衛尉伊策故皇太子之靈, 伊 is the envoy's name and 策 the announcement verb; treating "Yi Ce" as a personal name is wrong, and the proposed wording restores that parse.

translationRepairs.before: Though not born of the inner palace I served her as my own mother.
translationRepairs.after: Although I was not born to the empress, I served her as if she were my own mother.
translationRepairs.reason: The empress is the contextual referent of 中宮, not a building; the speaker contrasts not being born to her with serving her as his own mother.

translationRepairs.before: He claimed dutiful service to Jia despite birth.
translationRepairs.after: Though I was not born to the empress, I served her as though she were my own mother.
translationRepairs.reason: This restores the prince's own first-person letter and the filial comparison that the third-person summary omitted; the sentence does not supply a personal name.

translationRepairs.before: Since becoming crown prince edicts confined me—I could not see my mother.
translationRepairs.after: Since becoming crown prince, I have been kept under restrictions by decree and have not been allowed to see my mother.
translationRepairs.reason: The writer describes ordered restrictions since becoming crown prince and being unable to see his mother, without specifying house imprisonment.

translationRepairs.before: Palace rules barred him from Lady Xie.
translationRepairs.after: Since becoming crown prince, I have been kept under restrictions by decree and have not been allowed to see my mother.
translationRepairs.reason: First-person wording restores the decree and restrictions and says mother without adding a personal name not present in this sentence.

translationRepairs.before: Since Princess Dowager Xuan city died I received no comforting word—I constantly sat alone in empty rooms.
translationRepairs.after: Since the Lady of Yicheng died, I have received no care or concern, and have constantly sat in an empty room.
translationRepairs.reason: 宜城君 is the Lady of Yicheng; 存恤 is care or concern rather than necessarily a comforting word, and 空室 does not add a separate claim of solitude.

translationRepairs.before: Since the Lady of Yicheng died I received no comforting word—I constantly sat alone in empty rooms.
translationRepairs.after: Since the Lady of Yicheng died, I have received no care or concern, and have constantly sat in an empty room.
translationRepairs.reason: The sentence reports the writer's lack of care after the Lady of Yicheng's death and his constant sitting in an empty room, without asserting their kinship.

translationRepairs.before: The crown prince said, "Suddenly at night one must guard against the unexpected; one must not let firelight reveal the ruler's face."
translationRepairs.after: When the emperor asked why, the crown prince replied, "At night, in a sudden crisis, one must guard against the unexpected; the ruler should not be illuminated where others can see him."
translationRepairs.reason: The emperor asks why, and the prince warns against illumination during a sudden nighttime emergency; the proposed question is restored.

translationRepairs.before: He likened the heir to Sima Yi before court—reputation followed.
translationRepairs.after: He once told the assembled ministers that the crown prince resembled Emperor Xuan; the prince's good reputation spread throughout the realm.
translationRepairs.reason: The emperor tells assembled ministers the prince resembles Xuan; the prince’s reputation spreads.

translationRepairs.before: Empress Jia secretly ordered Yellow Gate eunuchs to flatter the crown prince: "Your Highness may indeed indulge every whim while still young—why bind yourself so tightly?"
translationRepairs.after: Empress Jia had long resented the crown prince's good reputation, so she secretly instructed the Yellow Gate eunuchs to flatter him: "Your Highness should indulge your desires while you are young. Why always restrain yourself?"
translationRepairs.reason: Jia resents the good reputation and secretly has the eunuchs encourage unrestrained behavior.

translationRepairs.before: When Consort Jiang bore a son they pushed costly toys and stipends—Yu complied.
translationRepairs.after: When the crown prince's favored Lady Jiang bore a son, they also urged lavish rewards and the making of many toys for the imperial grandson. The crown prince followed their advice.
translationRepairs.reason: The favored Jiang bears a son; the advisers urge rewards and toys for the grandson, and the prince follows them.

translationRepairs.before: He skipped audiences for back-garden games.
translationRepairs.after: His arrogance and laxity became increasingly evident; he sometimes neglected court attendance and was constantly playing in the rear garden.
translationRepairs.reason: The prince’s laxness becomes apparent; he sometimes skips attendance and habitually plays in the rear garden.

translationRepairs.before: He thrashed servants himself.
translationRepairs.after: If someone offended him, he beat that person with his own hands.
translationRepairs.reason: The victim is unspecified; he personally strikes people who offend him, not necessarily servants.

translationRepairs.before: Yet inside the palace he opened a market, had people butcher and sell ale, and weighed purchases in his own hands to the exact ounce.
translationRepairs.after: Yet he set up a market in the palace, had people butcher and sell liquor, and estimated weights with his own hand without error.
translationRepairs.reason: He has other people butcher and sell liquor and gauges weight by hand; direct butchering and coin weighing are not stated.

translationRepairs.before: Yet he ran a palace bazaar—himself butchering, selling ale, and weighing coin.
translationRepairs.after: Yet he set up a market in the palace, had others butcher and sell liquor, and could estimate an object's weight by hand without error.
translationRepairs.reason: He has other people butcher and sell liquor and gauges weight by hand; direct butchering and coin weighing are not stated.

translationRepairs.before: His mother's trade drew him to the stall.
translationRepairs.after: His mother was originally a butcher's daughter, which was why the crown prince enjoyed this.
translationRepairs.reason: His mother was a butcher’s daughter, offered as the explanation of his liking.

translationRepairs.before: The crown prince grew angry and had someone sew needles into Du Xi's usual felt mat to stab him.
translationRepairs.after: The crown prince grew angry and had someone place needles in Du Xi's usual felt mat to prick him.
translationRepairs.reason: He has another person put needles into Xi’s habitual felt seat; sewing and personal placement are not asserted.

translationRepairs.before: Yu pinned needles into Du Xi's seat cushion.
translationRepairs.after: Angered, the prince had needles placed in Du Xi's usual felt seat so that they would prick him.
translationRepairs.reason: He has another person put needles into Xi’s habitual felt seat; sewing and personal placement are not asserted.

translationRepairs.before: Guo Huai once pushed a Han match—Yu wanted it too.
translationRepairs.after: Earlier, Empress Jia's mother Guo Huai had wanted Han Shou's daughter to become crown princess, and the crown prince likewise wanted to marry into the Han family to strengthen his own position.
translationRepairs.reason: Guo Huai and the prince both desired Han Shou’s daughter as a match; he sought security for himself.

translationRepairs.before: Jia Wu and the empress forced Wang Yan's younger daughter Huifeng instead.
translationRepairs.after: But Han Shou's wife Jia Wu and the empress both refused; instead, they betrothed the crown prince to Wang Yan's younger daughter Huifeng.
translationRepairs.reason: Han Shou’s wife Jia Wu and the empress refuse and betroth him to Wang Yan’s younger daughter.

translationRepairs.before: Jia adopted the plot and smeared Yu empire-wide.
translationRepairs.after: The empress accepted what he said and spread accounts of the crown prince's faults far and wide.
translationRepairs.reason: The empress accepts the account and circulates the prince’s faults far and wide.

translationRepairs.before: Everyone saw Jia meant to kill the heir.
translationRepairs.after: People at court and throughout the country knew that Empress Jia intended to harm the crown prince.
translationRepairs.reason: Court and country know she intends to harm him; the wording does not overstate a specific killing method.

translationRepairs.before: Year nine saw an omen mulberry sprout west of the halls.
translationRepairs.after: In the sixth month of the ninth year, a mulberry sprouted in the western wing of the palace, grew more than a chi each day, and withered after several days.
translationRepairs.reason: The mulberry appears in the palace western wing, grows daily, and soon withers.

translationRepairs.before: She hid him, fed him wine and dates through Chen Wu until he was drunk.
translationRepairs.after: When he arrived, the empress did not see him but put him in a separate room. She sent the maid Chen Wu with wine and jujubes and pressed him to drink until he was drunk.
translationRepairs.reason: The empress does not meet him; maid Chen Wu brings wine and jujubes and makes him drunk.

translationRepairs.before: Blind drunk, he traced childish strokes.
translationRepairs.after: The crown prince, too drunk and confused to understand, copied it as directed, but half the characters were malformed.
translationRepairs.reason: He copies the text while drunk and unaware; half the characters are malformed.

translationRepairs.before: Helpers patched characters before Jia showed Hui.
translationRepairs.after: Afterward the incomplete characters were filled in, and the empress showed the text to the emperor.
translationRepairs.reason: The text is filled in and the empress presents it; the actor filling the characters is not invented.

translationRepairs.before: No one among lords and dukes spoke except Zhang Hua and Pei Wei who verified the crown prince's innocence.
translationRepairs.after: It was shown to all the princes and officials; none spoke except Zhang Hua and Pei Wei, who spoke in the crown prince's defense.
translationRepairs.reason: The material is shown to all the lords and princes; Zhang Hua and Pei Wei defend the heir.

translationRepairs.before: Silence fell until Zhang Hua and Pei Wei defended Yu.
translationRepairs.after: It was shown to all the princes and officials; none spoke except Zhang Hua and Pei Wei, who spoke in the crown prince's defense.
translationRepairs.reason: The material is shown to all the lords and princes; Zhang Hua and Pei Wei defend the heir.

translationRepairs.before: Jia feared delay—demoted Yu to commoner instead.
translationRepairs.after: Fearing that events might change, the empress submitted a memorial asking that the crown prince be reduced to commoner status; the emperor approved by edict.
translationRepairs.reason: Fearing a change in events she petitions to reduce him to a commoner and the edict permits it.

translationRepairs.before: Next New Year Jia staged a Yellow Gate confession implicating Yu.
translationRepairs.after: In the first month of the following year, Empress Jia again had a Yellow Gate attendant confess that he intended to rebel with the crown prince.
translationRepairs.reason: The empress has an attendant confess to an intention to rebel with the heir in the following first month.

translationRepairs.before: Luoyang read the staged confession.
translationRepairs.after: An edict circulated the attendant's confession among the dukes and ministers.
translationRepairs.reason: The edict circulates the confession to senior ministers, not the whole city.

translationRepairs.before: Wang Yan filed for divorce the moment Yu fell.
translationRepairs.after: Earlier, when the crown prince was deposed, his consort's father Wang Yan submitted a memorial requesting a divorce.
translationRepairs.reason: Wang Yan requests a divorce; this does not claim that divorce was completed.

translationRepairs.before: Injustice against Yu enraged the capital.
translationRepairs.after: The crown prince had been deposed for no fault of his own, and people were indignant.
translationRepairs.reason: The narrative expressly says the heir was deposed without fault and people were indignant.

translationRepairs.before: Right Guard Commandant Sima Ya, a distant kinsman of the imperial house, and Attendant Commandant Xu Chao, both favorites of the crown prince, grieved deeply; they told Sun Xiu, stratagemist to Prince Zhao of Lun: 'The state has no true heir—altar and grain will be imperiled; great ministers' disaster is sure to rise.
translationRepairs.after: Sima Ya, a commandant of the Right Guard and a distant member of the imperial clan, and Xu Chao, a commandant of the regular attendants, both enjoyed the crown prince's favor. Deeply grieved, they spoke to Sun Xiu, an adviser to Lun, Prince of Zhao: 'The state has no rightful heir, the altars of soil and grain will be endangered, and disaster will surely arise for the great ministers.
translationRepairs.reason: Sima Ya is distant imperial kin, both men favored by the prince, and Sun Xiu is adviser to Lun, Prince of Zhao; the speech stays open.

translationRepairs.before: Right Guard Commandant Sima Ya and Attendant Commandant Xu Chao, both favorites of the crown prince, grieved deeply; they told Sun Xiu, stratagemist to Prince Zhao of Lun: "The state has no true heir—altar and grain will be imperiled; great ministers' disaster is sure to rise.
translationRepairs.after: Sima Ya, a Right Guard commandant and distant member of the imperial clan, and Xu Chao, a commandant of the regular attendants, were both favored by the crown prince. Deeply grieved, they told Sun Xiu, an adviser to Lun, Prince of Zhao: "The state has no rightful heir; the dynasty is in danger, and disaster will surely come upon the great ministers.
translationRepairs.reason: Sima Ya is distant imperial kin, both men favored by the prince, and Sun Xiu is adviser to Lun, Prince of Zhao; the speech stays open.

translationRepairs.before: You serve the inner palace in the empress's confidence; all say you foreknew the crown prince's deposition—should trouble erupt, disaster will reach you too.
translationRepairs.after: You serve the inner palace and are close to Empress Jia; everyone says you knew of the crown prince's deposition beforehand. If trouble breaks out, disaster will surely reach you.
translationRepairs.reason: The speaker addresses the adviser directly: service to the palace, Jia’s closeness, foreknowledge, and danger are retained.

translationRepairs.before: They warned Sun Xiu that Jia would scapegoat Jia's allies.
translationRepairs.after: You serve the inner palace and are close to Empress Jia; everyone says you knew of the crown prince's deposition beforehand. If trouble breaks out, disaster will surely reach you.
translationRepairs.reason: The speaker addresses the adviser directly: service to the palace, Jia’s closeness, foreknowledge, and danger are retained.

translationRepairs.before: Xiu reported to Prince Zhao of Lun, and Lun accepted fully.
translationRepairs.after: Xiu told Lun, Prince of Zhao, who readily accepted the proposal.
translationRepairs.reason: Xiu tells Lun, Prince of Zhao, who accepts; the title is not a name “Zhao of Lun”.

translationRepairs.before: Sun Xiu sold the plot to Sima Lun.
translationRepairs.after: Sun Xiu told Sima Lun, Prince of Zhao, who readily accepted the proposal.
translationRepairs.reason: Xiu tells Lun, Prince of Zhao, who accepts; the title is not a name “Zhao of Lun”.

translationRepairs.before: Lun was branded Jia's man.
translationRepairs.after: You have long served Empress Jia, and people in the streets all call you a partisan of the Jia family.
translationRepairs.reason: The second Jia is the family or faction; the speaker addresses the prince who served the empress.

translationRepairs.before: Yu would not thank Lun for a late defection.
translationRepairs.after: Even if you now seek to do the crown prince a great service, though he might suppress his old resentment, he surely cannot reward you. He will think you changed sides under pressure from the people's expectations only to escape punishment.
translationRepairs.reason: The threatened prince may suppress his resentment but is predicted to withhold reward and view the reversal as self-protection.

translationRepairs.before: One slip and Lun's head would roll.
translationRepairs.after: If any fault should come to light, you would still not escape execution.
translationRepairs.reason: An exposed fault or pretext still leaves the addressee liable to execution.

translationRepairs.before: Better delay: Empress Jia is sure to harm the crown prince; then depose Jia, avenge the crown prince—merit enough to win your will.'
translationRepairs.after: Better to delay and postpone the appointed time. Empress Jia will surely harm the crown prince; then depose her and avenge him. That alone will be enough to count as a merit, and only then can you achieve your aim.'
translationRepairs.reason: The adviser recommends delay until Jia harms the heir, then deposing her and taking revenge to gain merit.

translationRepairs.before: Better delay: Empress Jia is sure to harm the crown prince; then depose Jia, avenge the crown prince—merit enough to win your will."
translationRepairs.after: Better to delay and postpone the appointed time. Empress Jia will surely harm the crown prince; then depose her and avenge him. That alone will be enough to count as a merit, and only then can you achieve your aim."
translationRepairs.reason: The adviser recommends delay until Jia harms the heir, then deposing her and taking revenge to gain merit.

translationRepairs.before: Sun Xiu spread rumors of a palace plot to restore Yu.
translationRepairs.after: Xiu then used counter-agents to spread word that people inside the palace meant to depose Empress Jia and welcome back the crown prince.
translationRepairs.reason: Counter-agents spread the reported palace intention; the report is not presented as an accomplished plot.

translationRepairs.before: Lü jailed and starved Yu; sympathizers smuggled food over walls.
translationRepairs.after: Lü told Liu Zhen, who moved the crown prince into a small compound and gave him no food at all; nevertheless, people in the palace passed food over the wall to the crown prince.
translationRepairs.reason: Lü informs Liu Zhen; Liu starves the heir in a small compound while people in the palace pass food over the wall.

translationRepairs.before: Sun Lü beat Yu to death in the latrine with a pestle—screams escaped.
translationRepairs.after: Lü then pressed the medicine on the crown prince, who refused to take it. When the crown prince went to the privy, Lü struck him dead with a medicine pestle. The crown prince cried out loudly, and his voice was heard outside.
translationRepairs.reason: The heir rejects the medicine, goes to the privy, is struck with the pestle and cries loudly.

translationRepairs.before: Though Yu's guilt was utmost he remains an imperial grandson—to dispatch him as a mere commoner truly pity—may Heaven grant kingly burial.
translationRepairs.after: Although Yu's guilt could scarcely be greater, he is still a descendant of the sovereign. To send him to burial as an ordinary commoner truly moves me to pity. I especially beg Your Majesty's grace to grant him the rites of a prince.
translationRepairs.reason: The literal is faithful to the memorial; the idiomatic must remain held while the preceding s0126 switches an open first-person speech into summary.

translationRepairs.before: I followed the testament and across set you up as heir to brighten our ancestors.
translationRepairs.after: In obedience to his final command, I established you as heir apparent, to bring glory to our ancestors.
translationRepairs.reason: The speaker follows the prior sovereign’s final wishes by establishing the heir to honor the ancestors; surrounding speech still needs coordinated editing.

translationRepairs.before: Hui claimed he installed Yu by Wu Di's will.
translationRepairs.after: In obedience to his final command, I established you as heir apparent, to bring glory to our ancestors.
translationRepairs.reason: The speaker follows the prior sovereign’s final wishes by establishing the heir to honor the ancestors; surrounding speech still needs coordinated editing.

translationRepairs.before: Hui likened the plot to classic wronged heirs.
translationRepairs.after: But I was blind to the vicious plotting, so that you suffered the calamity of an unnatural death: Shen Sheng and Xiao Ji have appeared again in our own day.
translationRepairs.reason: The speaker acknowledges blindness to the plot and compares the unjust death with Shen Sheng and Xiao Ji.

translationRepairs.before: He credited ministers for Jia's fall.
translationRepairs.after: Thanks to the wisdom of my ministers, and to the indignation of people and spirits, my mind was opened. I punished those responsible, and all received the penalty for their crimes.
translationRepairs.reason: Wise ministers and people’s and spirits’ indignation awaken the speaker, and the guilty are punished.

translationRepairs.before: What use mending poisoned wronged souls' cruel pain?
translationRepairs.after: But how can this lessen the cruel suffering of your unjustly afflicted spirit?
translationRepairs.reason: The question asks what relief this gives the unjustly afflicted soul and its suffering.

translationRepairs.before: Ritual could not unkill Yu.
translationRepairs.after: But how can this lessen the cruel suffering of your unjustly afflicted spirit?
translationRepairs.reason: The question asks what relief this gives the unjustly afflicted soul and its suffering.

translationRepairs.before: Imperial rhetoric of inner ache.
translationRepairs.after: Thus grief and regret shake me to my innermost being.
translationRepairs.reason: Grief and regret shake the speaker inwardly.

translationRepairs.before: When the hearse set out great wind and thunder came—canopies and coverings flew torn.
translationRepairs.after: When the funeral procession set out, a great wind arose with thunder and lightning, and its curtains and canopies were blown apart.
translationRepairs.reason: Wind, thunder and lightning arise when the funeral sets out and curtains and canopies are blown apart.

translationRepairs.before: Storm shattered funeral umbrellas.
translationRepairs.after: When the funeral procession set out, a great wind arose with thunder and lightning, and its curtains and canopies were blown apart.
translationRepairs.reason: Wind, thunder and lightning arise when the funeral sets out and curtains and canopies are blown apart.

translationRepairs.before: You drew from youth heroic sap, fragrance ripe at birth.
translationRepairs.after: From childhood you were endowed with outstanding gifts; your fragrant virtue grew luxuriant.
translationRepairs.reason: The lament praises exceptional qualities in youth through the metaphor of burgeoning fragrance.

translationRepairs.before: Praise for childhood brilliance.
translationRepairs.after: From childhood you were endowed with outstanding gifts; your fragrant virtue grew luxuriant.
translationRepairs.reason: The lament praises exceptional qualities in youth through the metaphor of burgeoning fragrance.

translationRepairs.before: Wu Di's praise.
translationRepairs.after: Long ago your sage ancestor prized your goodness and fine qualities.
translationRepairs.reason: The sage ancestor admired the addressee’s fine qualities.

translationRepairs.before: Therefore we installed you heir to light imperial foundations forever.
translationRepairs.after: Therefore you were established as heir, to continue the imperial foundation forever.
translationRepairs.reason: The addressee is established as heir to continue the imperial foundation.

translationRepairs.before: Heir establishment recalled.
translationRepairs.after: Therefore you were established as heir, to continue the imperial foundation forever.
translationRepairs.reason: The addressee is established as heir to continue the imperial foundation.

translationRepairs.before: Rhetorical grief at murder.
translationRepairs.after: How could the cruel and violent secretly plot, bringing calamity like this?
translationRepairs.reason: The lament asks how cruel forces could plot secretly and cause such calamity.

translationRepairs.before: Seasonal mourning tropes.
translationRepairs.after: Sorrow moves the harmonious breath of nature; anguish reaches through the four seasons.
translationRepairs.reason: Grief affects harmonious qi and pain reaches across the seasons, retaining the image.

translationRepairs.before: Funeral lament pause.
translationRepairs.after: Alas, how sorrowful!
translationRepairs.reason: The words are an exclamation of sorrow.

translationRepairs.before: Hui blamed himself.
translationRepairs.after: That you were degraded and deposed was truly due to my blindness.
translationRepairs.reason: The speaker acknowledges personal lack of discernment in the deposition.

translationRepairs.before: Universal mourning asserted.
translationRepairs.after: Among all those who possess understanding, who is not stricken with grief?
translationRepairs.reason: The rhetorical question asks who among people of understanding does not grieve.

translationRepairs.before: Justice spans dynasties.
translationRepairs.after: Though the ages differ, the pattern is the same; past and present follow one principle.
translationRepairs.reason: The cases occur in different ages but follow the same pattern and principle.

translationRepairs.before: Tomb closure comforts ghost.
translationRepairs.after: The burial chamber has now been prepared, and your spirit will be laid to rest.
translationRepairs.reason: The burial chamber has been prepared so the spirit may find rest.

translationRepairs.before: Mourning cortège splendor.
translationRepairs.after: A vast array of feathered canopies; rank upon rank of officials.
translationRepairs.reason: Feathered canopies are expansive and officials are arrayed in order; no unsupported plumes are added.

translationRepairs.before: Courtiers weep together.
translationRepairs.after: All share the same grief and pain: who does not feel bitter sorrow?
translationRepairs.reason: Shared grief and pain prompt a rhetorical question about sorrow.

translationRepairs.before: Canonized Crown Prince Minhuai.
translationRepairs.after: He was given the posthumous name Minhuai.
translationRepairs.reason: 湣懷 is a posthumous name, not religious canonization.

translationRepairs.before: Buried sixth month at Xianping.
translationRepairs.after: On the jimao day of the sixth month, he was buried at Xianping Mausoleum.
translationRepairs.reason: The burial is stated as jimao in the sixth month at Xianping; the textual day conflict remains a date-audit issue.

translationRepairs.before: Second son Zang, styled Jingwen.
translationRepairs.after: Zang's courtesy name was Jingwen.
translationRepairs.reason: The source states Zang’s courtesy name Jingwen without explicitly ranking him as second son.

translationRepairs.before: Yongkang fourth month made Linhuai prince.
translationRepairs.after: In the fourth month of Yongkang's first year, he was enfeoffed Prince of Linhuai.
translationRepairs.reason: He is enfeoffed Prince of Linhuai in the fourth month of Yongkang’s first year.

translationRepairs.before: Zang named grand-heir.
translationRepairs.after: Now I establish Zang as imperial grandson-heir.
translationRepairs.reason: The edict establishes Zang as imperial grandson-heir.

translationRepairs.before: Eastern Palace staff transferred to grand-heir posts.
translationRepairs.after: The crown prince's officials shall immediately become officials of the imperial grandson-heir.
translationRepairs.reason: The crown prince’s officials are transferred to serve the grandson-heir.

translationRepairs.before: Staff slid from heir to grand-heir titles.
translationRepairs.after: The crown prince's officials shall immediately become officials of the imperial grandson-heir.
translationRepairs.reason: The crown prince’s officials are transferred to serve the grandson-heir.

translationRepairs.before: Prince Zhao of Lun acted Grand Tutor to the imperial grandson-heir.'
translationRepairs.after: Lun, Prince of Zhao, shall act as Grand Mentor to the imperial grandson-heir.'
translationRepairs.reason: Lun, Prince of Zhao, is to act as the grandson-heir’s Grand Mentor; the edict closes here.

translationRepairs.before: Prince Zhao of Lun acted Grand Tutor to the imperial grandson-heir."
translationRepairs.after: Lun, Prince of Zhao, shall act as Grand Mentor to the imperial grandson-heir."
translationRepairs.reason: Lun, Prince of Zhao, is to act as the grandson-heir’s Grand Mentor; the edict closes here.

translationRepairs.before: Luoyang wept along Bronze Camel Street.
translationRepairs.after: When they reached Bronze Camel Street, the palace attendants wept, the attendants all sobbed, and passersby wiped away their tears.
translationRepairs.reason: Palace people weep, accompanying attendants sob, and passersby wipe tears at Bronze Camel Street.

translationRepairs.before: The mulberry sprouted again west of the wing; when the grand heir was deposed it withered.
translationRepairs.after: The mulberry tree grew again in the western wing; when the imperial grandson was deposed, it withered.
translationRepairs.reason: The mulberry grows again in the western wing and withers after the grandson is deposed.

translationRepairs.before: Omen mulberry mirrored heir's fall.
translationRepairs.after: The mulberry tree grew again in the western wing; when the imperial grandson was deposed, it withered.
translationRepairs.reason: The mulberry grows again in the western wing and withers after the grandson is deposed.

translationRepairs.before: In the first month of Yongning year one Prince Zhao of Lun usurped the throne, degrading him to Prince of Puyang—together with the emperor he moved to Jinyong and soon after was murdered.
translationRepairs.after: In the first month of Yongning's first year, Lun, Prince of Zhao, usurped the throne. He reduced the grandson to Prince of Puyang; the grandson and the emperor were both moved to Jinyong, and the grandson was killed soon afterward.
translationRepairs.reason: Lun usurps the throne and reduces the grandson to Prince of Puyang, then the grandson moves with the emperor and is killed.

translationRepairs.before: Yongning coup demoted Zang—murdered at Jinyong.
translationRepairs.after: In the first month of Yongning's first year, Lun, Prince of Zhao, usurped the throne. He reduced the grandson to Prince of Puyang; the grandson and the emperor were both moved to Jinyong, and the grandson was killed soon afterward.
translationRepairs.reason: Lun usurps the throne and reduces the grandson to Prince of Puyang, then the grandson moves with the emperor and is killed.

translationRepairs.before: Tai'an era canonized Ai.
translationRepairs.after: Early in Tai'an he was posthumously given the name Ai.
translationRepairs.reason: Ai is a name posthumously conferred early in Tai’an.

translationRepairs.before: Editors praise Yu's childhood gifts.
translationRepairs.after: The historian says: Minhuai showed a remarkably intelligent bearing and a precociously mature nature.
translationRepairs.reason: The historian praises Minhuai’s intelligence and early maturity.

translationRepairs.before: The realm expected greatness.
translationRepairs.after: All under Heaven turned their hearts toward him and had considerable hopes for his future.
translationRepairs.reason: The realm turns its heart toward him and has hopes of what is to come.

translationRepairs.before: Hui's blindness and court cowardice blamed.
translationRepairs.after: The ruler lacked the discernment to uncover what was hidden, and none of the many officials showed the integrity of a remonstrating minister.
translationRepairs.reason: The ruler lacks the ability to uncover hidden matters and officials lack the integrity to remonstrate.

translationRepairs.before: Though mourning rites ran full and grief ran deep, what did they mend for the poisoned innocent!
translationRepairs.after: Although the rites of mourning and honor were complete and the grief and pity profound, how could they help the one who had suffered such cruelty?
translationRepairs.reason: Funeral honors and profound sorrow cannot undo the sufferer’s cruel fate.

translationRepairs.before: Posthumous honors could not resurrect him.
translationRepairs.after: Although the rites of mourning and honor were complete and the grief and pity profound, how could they help the one who had suffered such cruelty?
translationRepairs.reason: Funeral honors and profound sorrow cannot undo the sufferer’s cruel fate.

translationRepairs.before: Verse praises innate wit.
translationRepairs.after: The encomium says: Minhuai was intelligent and perceptive, truly endowed by Heaven.
translationRepairs.reason: The encomium praises Minhuai’s intelligence as heaven-endowed.

translationRepairs.before: Court awaited his reign.
translationRepairs.after: His imperial grandfather treasured him; the assembled officials craned their necks in expectation.
translationRepairs.reason: The grandfather cherishes him and officials crane their necks in anticipation.

translationRepairs.before: Death ended every hope of restoration.
translationRepairs.after: Once he fell victim to ruthless cruelty, hope for his return was in vain.
translationRepairs.reason: He falls victim to ruthless cruelty and hope for his return becomes vain.

translationRepairs.before: Astrologers said Guangling bore an emperor's aura, so Yu was made Prince of Guangling with fifty thousand households.
translationRepairs.after: At the time observers of portents said Guangling had the aura of a Son of Heaven, so he was enfeoffed Prince of Guangling, with a fief of fifty thousand households.
translationRepairs.reason: The portent observers describe an imperial aura in Guangling and he receives its princely title and fifty thousand households.

translationRepairs.before: The court recruited eminent tutors—He Shao as Grand Tutor, Wang Rong as Grand Mentor, Yang Ji as Grand Guardian, Pei Kai as Junior Tutor, Zhang Hua as Junior Mentor, and He Qiao as Junior Guardian.
translationRepairs.after: The court made an extensive selection of men of virtue and standing as his tutors and guardians: He Shao as Grand Tutor, Wang Rong as Grand Mentor, Yang Ji as Grand Guardian, Pei Kai as Junior Tutor, Zhang Hua as Junior Mentor, and He Qiao as Junior Guardian.
translationRepairs.reason: The six named men are appointed to the senior and junior tutor, mentor and guardian offices.

translationRepairs.before: In Yongkang fourth month he was made Prince of Xiangyang.
translationRepairs.after: In the fourth month of Yongkang's first year, he was enfeoffed Prince of Xiangyang.
translationRepairs.reason: He is enfeoffed Prince of Xiangyang in the fourth month of Yongkang’s first year.

translationRepairs.before: In Yongning eighth month he was made imperial grandson-heir.
translationRepairs.after: In the eighth month of Yongning's first year, he was established as imperial grandson-heir.
translationRepairs.reason: He is established as imperial grandson-heir in the eighth month of Yongning’s first year.

translationRepairs.before: Thereupon Minister Director He Yu was dispatched with insignia, Xie Jie as deputy, together with General-in-Chief Prince Liang of Liang, Eastern Garrison Prince Huainan of Yun, Forward General Eastern Martial Duke Dan, Prince Zhao of Lun, and Grand Tutor He Shao to the Eastern Palace to depose the crown prince as commoner.
translationRepairs.after: Thereupon Minister Director He Yu was dispatched with insignia, Xie Jie as deputy, together with General-in-Chief Rong, Prince of Liang, Eastern Garrison General Yun, Prince of Huainan, Forward General Eastern Martial Duke Dan, Lun, Prince of Zhao, and Grand Guardian He Shao to the Eastern Palace to depose the crown prince as commoner.
translationRepairs.reason: 梁王肜 is Rong, Prince of Liang, and 允 is Yun, Prince of Huainan, but 太保何劭 is He Shao the Grand Guardian, not Grand Tutor; preserve the name corrections and correct this additional office.

translationRepairs.before: Thereupon Minister Director He Yu was dispatched with insignia, with Xie Jie as deputy, together with General-in-Chief Sima Tong, Prince of Liang; Eastern Garrison General Sima Yun, Prince of Huainan; Forward General Sima Dan, Eastern Martial Duke; Sima Lun, Prince of Zhao; and Grand Tutor He Shao. They went to the Eastern Palace to depose the Crown Prince as a commoner.
translationRepairs.after: Thereupon Minister Director He Yu was dispatched with insignia, with Xie Jie as deputy, together with General-in-Chief Sima Rong, Prince of Liang; Eastern Garrison General Sima Yun, Prince of Huainan; Forward General Sima Dan, Eastern Martial Duke; Sima Lun, Prince of Zhao; and Grand Guardian He Shao. They went to the Eastern Palace to depose the Crown Prince as a commoner.
translationRepairs.reason: 梁王肜 is Rong, Prince of Liang, and 允 is Yun, Prince of Huainan, but 太保何劭 is He Shao the Grand Guardian, not Grand Tutor; preserve the name corrections and correct this additional office.

translationRepairs.before: Dan escorted Crown Princess Wang and three imperial grandsons to Jinyong with armed guards, interrogated Consort-in-chief Xie and heir guardian Jiang Jun to death.
translationRepairs.after: Dan had Crown Princess Wang and the three imperial grandsons escorted to Jinyong City under armed guard; Consort Shufei Xie and Jiang Jun, a baolin of the crown prince, were interrogated to death.
translationRepairs.reason: Reconsidering 澹以兵仗送 and 考竟, the source attributes the escort to Dan but does not establish his personal presence; passive phrasing also avoids assigning who personally conducted the fatal interrogation. 保林 is a rank, not an heir guardian.

translationRepairs.before: Dan marched Wang consort and grandsons to Jinyong—executed Xie and Jiang Jun.
translationRepairs.after: Dan had Crown Princess Wang and the three imperial grandsons escorted to Jinyong City under armed guard; Consort Shufei Xie and Jiang Jun, a crown prince’s consort of the rank of baolin, were interrogated to death.
translationRepairs.reason: The concise source associates Dan with the armed escort without specifying personal presence, and does not name the interrogators. This revision preserves that uncertainty while retaining 考竟 and the consort rank 保林.

translationRepairs.before: When Deposed Commoner Jia died, they executed Liu Zhen, Sun Lü, Cheng Ju, and others, and posthumously restored the crown prince; the edict read: 'The emperor dispatches the credential-bearer, concurrent Director of Works, Commandant of the Guard Yi Ce to the spirit of the late crown prince: Alas!
translationRepairs.after: When Deposed Commoner Jia died, they executed Liu Zhen, Sun Lü, Cheng Ju, and others, and restored the crown prince by patent, saying: “The emperor sends an envoy bearing the credentials, Commandant of the Guard Yi, concurrently serving as Director of Works, to announce by patent to the spirit of the late crown prince: Alas!
translationRepairs.reason: 持節 describes the envoy bearing a token of official authority; credentials preserves its function without implying a numerical tally. 伊 is the envoy’s name and 策 is the patent action, not part of that name.

translationRepairs.before: In youth you bore a nature quick and wise; the late emperor gave you exceptional favor, opening great territory, holding Hailing.
translationRepairs.after: In youth you bore a nature quick and wise; you received the late emperor’s extraordinary favor. Your domain was greatly opened, and you came to possess Huailing.
translationRepairs.reason: 淮陵 is Huailing, not Hailing. The parallel phrases describe the opening of the domain and possession of Huailing without explicitly assigning both actions to the late emperor.

translationRepairs.before: Hui's ghost-eulogy praised Wu Di's love and Yu's fief.
translationRepairs.after: From youth you showed remarkable intelligence and received the late emperor’s extraordinary favor. Your domain was greatly expanded, and you came to possess Huailing.
translationRepairs.reason: The speech directly addresses the deceased, and 淮陵 is Huailing. The source does not explicitly say that the late emperor personally granted both territorial actions.

translationRepairs.before: In the fourth month posthumous investiture as Prince of Nanyang.
translationRepairs.after: In the fourth month, he was posthumously enfeoffed as Prince of Nanyang.
translationRepairs.reason: 追封 means posthumous enfeoffment; 四月 gives the fourth month. The preceding unit identifies the deceased subject, although its missing written name remains a separate source issue.

translationRepairs.before: Fourth month titled Prince of Nanyang.
translationRepairs.after: In the fourth month, he was posthumously made Prince of Nanyang.
translationRepairs.reason: 追封 is a posthumous grant of title. The preceding unit provides the deceased subject; this decision does not repair or settle its missing name.
